name: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
title: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
answer: Lighting rigs and relighting in AI photography and hyper-realism cover the placement, intensity, color, and shape of virtual light sources in a scene, and the process of changing how an existing image is lit without rebuilding the scene. This includes studio-style key, fill, rim, and practical lights, environment maps for reflections, and relighting a portrait or product shot from a single photograph. The goal is to make synthetic or edited images match the physical behavior of light on skin, fabric, glass, and metal.

sections.body: Lighting rigs and relighting in AI photography and hyper-realism cover the placement, intensity, color, and shape of virtual light sources in a scene, and the process of changing how an existing image is lit without rebuilding the scene. This includes studio-style key, fill, rim, and practical lights, environment maps for reflections, and relighting a portrait or product shot from a single photograph. The goal is to make synthetic or edited images match the physical behavior of light on skin, fabric, glass, and metal.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on standard GPU workstations and cloud render farms, with most interactive relighting tools using a game engine or a neural network running in a browser or desktop app. A typical pipeline stores a base color image, a depth map, a normal map, and a material or roughness map, then computes new lighting from those channels. Training and inference for learned relighting models require the same class of hardware used for image generation, often a single high-memory consumer or data-center GPU for interactive work.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common approach is to decompose an image into albedo, normals, and lighting, then recombine them under a new light rig. Neural relighting models are trained on pairs of images of the same subject under many known lighting conditions, often captured in a light stage. For synthetic scenes, artists place virtual lights in a 3D viewport and the renderer or neural shader updates the image in real time. The work is iterative: an artist adjusts light angle, color temperature, softness, and falloff until the highlights and shadows match the intended look.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Relighting raises provenance questions because a single photograph can be altered to suggest a different time of day, location, or studio setup, which matters for journalism, evidence, and advertising. Rights issues arise when a model is trained on copyrighted photographs or when a relit image is used without disclosing the edit. The site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, and while most are not specific to relighting, the same questions about training data and derivative works apply. A working professional should keep the original plate and the lighting metadata so an edit can be reviewed.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward fully controllable relighting from a single phone photo, with sliders for sun position, softbox size, and colored gels that update in real time. Video relighting is becoming practical, allowing a moving subject to be relit consistently across frames. As models improve, the distinction between a physical light rig and a neural one will blur, and photographers may treat a lighting setup as a reusable preset that can be applied to any subject after the shoot.
